## Purpose {.unnumbered .unlisted}

_Why can training on a useful recovery record teach the model to repeat the mistake instead of the correction?_

While prompt engineering and runtime guardrails guide an off-the-shelf model, fine-tuning modifies the neural network weights directly, embedding specialized decision policies and tool calling conventions into model parameters. However, training on multi-turn trajectories requires strict separation between agent proposals and external environment observations: for trajectory imitation, loss applies only to selected policy responses, while environment feedback remains conditioning context. Naive fine-tuning can teach a policy to hallucinate its own tool responses or overfit to static workspace layouts, degrading general reasoning and error recovery. Systems engineering governs how datasets are partitioned, how loss masks are applied, and how updated checkpoints are validated against regression suites before deployment. An update is worth releasing only when closed-loop task acceptance improves under the same runtime that still bounds every proposal the model makes, however far its training loss has fallen.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

\newpage

:::

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}

- Assign agent behavior to weights, context, or runtime, and decide when a failure warrants a weight change
- Construct model inputs that preserve intended conditioning and price per-invocation serialization in training tokens
- Map admitted response spans to causal token targets, observation masks, and termination policy
- Compare loss weighting and construct batches without unintended cross-example dependencies
- Calculate imitation regret bounds on reference and learner states to decide when on-policy labeling pays
- Calculate preference margins and gradient weights, and distinguish what a comparison measures from task acceptance
- Select behavior sources and parameter artifacts using explicit resource and version accounting
- Evaluate a versioned policy for release on closed-loop acceptance, cost per accepted task, and schema transfer, while preserving runtime enforcement

:::

## Recovery Records as Training Data {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-introduction}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/hsa_locator_origin.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H·S·A locator with no axis highlighted and the origin dot highlighted in purple."}

*Fine-tuning reshapes each model call but leaves every exposure to the runtime.*
:::

Consider a recovery demonstration admitted by the curation pipeline for the repair agent (lighthouse \ref{lhs-vol3-repair-agent}) into `repair_demonstrations_v1`. During the recorded session, the agent generated a malformed edit proposal that the runtime validator refused prior to tool dispatch. In response to the failure notification, the model inspected the tool schema, generated a corrected edit, and produced candidate patch `ws_r20`. From this multi-turn trajectory, the target-selection policy `recovery_targets_v1` marks three assistant turns as supervised targets: the schema inspection request (`e3`), the corrected edit (`e4`), and the scoped final summary (`e6`). The malformed proposal (`e2`) and the runtime's refusal remain in the input history as conditioning context. The member that entered the corpus is the redacted view `trace_r19_01_redacted_v1`, and the corpus manifest binds it to those role assignments, its lineage, and its split membership.

An admitted record is not yet in a form a training loop can safely ingest. The raw event log is an interleaved transcript of heterogeneous events, recording model generations, runtime observations, and tool responses in the exact sequence they occurred. If a data loader treats every assistant message as a supervised target, it computes loss on the malformed edit proposal alongside the correction, directly reinforcing the initial mistake. If the training pipeline computes loss across all sequence tokens indiscriminately, the model expends parameter capacity predicting deterministic environment replies, such as compiler diagnostics or file directory listings, that the model will never emit during inference. If the batching pipeline packs multiple trajectories into a shared context window without attention masking, self-attention heads attend across sample boundaries, leaking private workspace contents into unrelated training examples. Standard cross-entropy loss fails silently under each of these conditions. The empirical loss decreases steadily as the optimizer fits the data, concealing severe behavioral corruption from offline training metrics. While curation contracts determine which actions demonstrate desirable behavior and evaluation contracts measure the deployed agent, neither specifies how to convert a multi-turn execution trace into isolated, causal gradient updates.

The path from an admitted record to an evaluated policy update begins with a question curation leaves open, namely which parts of the repair behavior belong in weights at all (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-scope). The answer fixes what the data pipeline must protect. Serialization reconstructs each model input exactly as the agent received it (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-serialization), loss masking places the gradient on the selected responses and nowhere else (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-loss-masking), and batching shares buffers without letting examples read one another or skew one another's weight (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-batching). Masking and batching guard directly against the three silent failures above, and serialization guards the premise both rely on, that each prefix is the one the model actually saw.

A faithful loader still trains on recorded prefixes, and the deployed policy acts on prefixes its own choices produce. Exposure bias prices that gap over the horizon and decides when labeling the learner's own states pays (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-exposure-bias), and schema robustness asks the same question of the tool interfaces the policy is shown (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-schemas). The remaining sections vary the update itself along three independent choices: the objective, where preference optimization contrasts valid alternatives that imitation cannot rank (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-dpo); the behavior source, where distillation moves a costlier configuration's behavior into a cheaper one (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-distillation); and the parameter artifact, where adapters change what a run must store (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-peft). Closed-loop evaluation decides whether any of them earned a release (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-benchmarking), and a training manifest for the repair policy assembles the whole chain (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-synthesis).

## Scope of Supervised Fine-Tuning {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-scope}

Modifying model weights is an expensive, high-blast-radius intervention reserved for specific failure modes. The intervention ladder orders changes by cost and reversibility, so engineers consider cheaper prompt, schema, and runtime mitigations before committing compute to parameter updates, while diagnostic evidence can justify a direct weight update. Supervised fine-tuning can address systematic behavioral defects rooted in the policy itself rather than omitted instructions or missing runtime constraints. The principle of verified trajectory post-training (principle \ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training})\index{Principle!verified trajectory post-training} requires curation to relate the recorded evidence to a declared learning use and distinguish admissible targets from contextual or rejected actions. While this ordering serves as a defensive default justified by operational cost and blast radius, @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-distillation examines the complementary scenario where fine-tuning proves more economical than paying the recurring token latency and cost of carrying lengthy guidance in every prompt.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The intervention ladder, which orders context, schema, runtime, and parameter interventions by cost and reversibility, is established in @sec-vol3-flywheel-intervention-order.
:::

**Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)**\index{Supervised fine-tuning!definition} adjusts trainable model parameters to maximize the conditional likelihood of selected target tokens given their causal prefix context. When processing an admitted trajectory record such as `trace_r19_01_redacted_v1`, the training loop must implement the specific recovery sequence defined in `recovery_targets_v1` rather than indiscriminately computing loss over every recorded token. The model must observe the historical context and tool outputs that justify a chosen action, yet the data pipeline must strictly censor subsequent execution steps that would prematurely reveal future observations or solutions. Trajectory fine-tuning therefore inherits two distinct data contracts: a *target-selection contract* that designates which tokens contribute to the loss gradient, and a *conditioning contract* that governs what causal history the model observes when generating those tokens.

This distinction defines what it means for an agent to learn improved behavior rather than overfit an idiosyncratic run. In an error-recovery trajectory, the true behavioral goal is teaching the model to inspect an updated schema after encountering a refusal, issue a properly formed corrective call, and interpret what the runtime verification check establishes. Merely memorizing the file paths of a specific test fixture or predicting hard-coded test outputs minimizes training loss without acquiring generalizable recovery skills. Evaluating whether the updated policy transfers these procedural habits to unfamiliar environments and novel tasks is precisely what @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-benchmarking measures.

### Procedure, contracts, and enforcement {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-behavior-homes}

Every response generated by an agent emerges from two inputs: the model's static weights and the dynamic context window assembled for that invocation. Because fine-tuning updates only the weights, system architects must divide agent capabilities into three architectural homes, summarized in @tbl-vol3-fine-tuning-scope:

* *Procedure* represents behavior that remains stable across tasks and evolves slowly, such as inspecting diagnostic output before modifying source code or auditing unresolved issues before reporting task completion. Procedure is what model weights can reliably internalize.
* *Contracts* represent the dynamic operational facts that vary across deployments, user sessions, and individual execution turns, such as API tool definitions, schema requirements, environment parameters, and granted permissions. Contracts belong strictly in the prompt context; a model that has memorized an earlier schema will continue emitting obsolete arguments when an interface changes.
* *Enforcement* represents the critical invariants that must hold even when the model generates incorrect or adversarial proposals, such as schema validation, authorization checks, sandbox containment, and execution timeouts. Enforcement must reside in the deterministic runtime harness under invariant closure (principle \ref{pri-invariant-closure}).

| Home    | Intended responsibility                                                                    | Consequence for fine-tuning                                                                                                      |
|:--------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Weights | Learned procedures and response tendencies, including tool selection and recovery behavior | Update the proposal distribution, then measure whether the changed behavior helps under the declared task conditions             |
| Context | Current task facts, tool schemas, observations, and represented scope                      | Supply the information the policy needs now; do not rely on memorized versions as the authority for current facts or permissions |
| Runtime | Validation, authorization, containment, resource controls, and evidence collection         | Preserve enforcement independently of the learned policy; a model's predicted result is not an observed external effect          |

: **Responsibilities of Weights, Context, and Runtime**: Weights hold procedure, context holds the current contract, and the runtime enforces that contract whatever the model proposes. {#tbl-vol3-fine-tuning-scope}

Relying on parameters to store interface contracts creates immediate operational brittleness. When a tool interface adds a required parameter or alters its return structure, a model that relies on memorized signatures will continue generating obsolete calls. Similarly, a revoked authorization remains revoked regardless of how frequently the action appeared in successful training demonstrations. Fine-tuning cannot replace dynamic contracts; what it can teach is the procedural discipline of consulting and adhering to whichever contract the context window specifies.

This architectural boundary disproves the naive view that fine-tuning simply moves the prompt into the weights. Only the procedural components of a prompt (structured reasoning guidelines, diagnostic checklists, or few-shot error recovery examples) can be absorbed into the parameters, saving substantial token overhead on every turn (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-distillation). The contractual components must remain in the prompt context, because omitting them forces the model to guess the operational facts of the current execution environment. Furthermore, the deterministic checks that enforce authorization and boundary invariants cannot reside in either prompts or weights, because probabilistic token distributions cannot guarantee invariant execution.

Fine-tuning alters the policy's proposal distribution: which tools it requests, how thoroughly it investigates diagnostic evidence, and which execution paths it explores. These behavioral shifts directly influence task success rates, end-to-end latency, and token consumption. Nevertheless, every proposed action executes entirely within the execution horizons, state machines, and authority boundaries established by the runtime harness. This separation is the *proposal boundary*. Training reshapes what the policy proposes, while the runtime decides which actions are permitted to execute. This principle governs every adaptation strategy in this chapter, culminating in the release verification criteria.

### Objective, behavior source, and artifact {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-adaptation-choices}

Designing an adaptation pipeline requires making three orthogonal decisions:

* **Training Objective**: The loss formulation that defines the learning signal. Supervised imitation learning maximizes the likelihood of curated target demonstrations, whereas preference learning techniques such as direct preference optimization (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-dpo) optimize policy weights by contrasting preferred trajectories against dispreferred alternatives under an explicit ranking criterion.
* **Behavior Source**: The origin of the demonstrations and environmental conditioning. Traces may be harvested from instrumented production systems and filtered through offline verification, generated by a teacher configuration with privileged context or an expanded search budget (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-distillation), labeled on the states the learner itself reaches, or synthesized by injecting faults the recordings never contained (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-dagger).
* **Parameter Artifact**: The physical representation of the updated weights. Teams can fine-tune all model parameters directly or train modular adapter matrices, such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) modules, that attach to a frozen base checkpoint (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-peft).

Because these three design dimensions are orthogonal, they combine modularly: a deployment might train a lightweight parameter adapter using a direct preference objective derived from synthetic teacher demonstrations.

Regardless of which combination an architecture adopts, the training process depends fundamentally on how trajectory records are converted into model inputs. Serialization determines tokenization and visibility windows, loss masking isolates the precise prediction targets, and batching schedules balance gradient variance across variable-length interaction turns. When deployed, the trained artifact will inevitably encounter unseen environmental states and revised tool schemas, requiring empirical validation before release. Constructing the prefix input and conditioning window for each targeted response constitutes the initial systems hurdle.

## Serializing Trajectories {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-serialization}

Consider the repair demonstration admitted during curation: it contains a malformed edit proposal, a runtime refusal, a schema inspection, and a corrected edit. A training loader that strips out the refusal fundamentally alters the problem the subsequent correction answered. Similarly, a loader that places a later passing test check before the edit leaks future evidence that the model never possessed when proposing the patch. While curation identifies which model completions are worthy of reinforcement, serialization must reconstruct the exact prompt and observation history that elicited them. This includes preserving any runtime redactions, such as synthetic placeholders substituted for private file paths, so the training example faithfully reflects the environment the model actually encountered.

### Reconstructing each model input {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-input-reconstruction}

Runtime event logs record system state transitions, but an event log alone does not guarantee what was present in a model's context window. System prompts evolve, tool schemas update dynamically, and intermediate messages are often summarized or truncated to fit token budgets. To reconstruct inputs accurately, the training pipeline relies on delivered-input manifests. These manifests identify the exact messages, tool definitions, summaries, and bounded observations dispatched to the model, along with their contents and schema versions. The manifest provides the authoritative record that a specific payload entered an invocation, preventing accidental data leakage or historical revisionism.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The delivered-input manifest that records the exact payload sent to the model, rather than mutable paths or references, is established in @sec-vol3-durable-execution-event-schema.
:::

When constructing an example that demands historical fidelity, serialize the selected invocation directly from this recorded manifest. The example must preserve the observation exactly as the agent saw it, including partial buffers, truncated outputs, or execution errors, rather than substituting a clean or complete result obtained later in the run. Conversely, when intentionally transforming an example, apply the reviewed transformation systematically to both the prompt and the associated response, retain parent trace references, and recheck schema compatibility. Shortening prompts for context distillation (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-distillation) is one such transformation.

@Tbl-vol3-serialization-repair-spans outlines how curated responses map to their valid conditioning context in the running repair demonstration. While the table highlights the core causal dependencies, the fully rendered training example incorporates the entire context available at that turn, including system instructions and active tool definitions.

| Selected response | Relevant conditioning evidence                                                                      | Response content selected by curation                |
|:------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|
| `e3`              | Earlier delivered task context and the malformed `e2` proposal with its pre-dispatch refusal        | Request to inspect the available schema              |
| `e4`              | The corresponding returned schema and the retained context supporting the edit                      | Corrected edit with its version condition            |
| `e6`              | The candidate-specific check summary delivered at `e5` and retained evidence for the report's scope | Final report of the supported result and limitations |

: **Inputs and Selected Responses in the Repair Demonstration**: Each row pairs a reviewed response with evidence available to condition it. {#tbl-vol3-serialization-repair-spans}

Notice the causal boundaries across these turns. The refusal at `e2` demonstrates that runtime validation caught the malformed proposal before dispatch; no tool executed on the host. The check summary at `e5` arrived only after the agent issued the corrected edit, so it can condition the final report at `e6`, but cannot appear in the context for `e4`. Similarly, selecting the schema inspection at `e3` isolates the model's query tokens for training while treating the returned schema as external observation. Maintaining these explicit associations ensures that subsequent loss masking isolates model decisions from environment observations.

### Rendering with versioned templates {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-template-rendering}

Before training begins, structured message objects (system instructions, user prompts, assistant thoughts, tool calls, and environment returns) must be serialized into the token sequence expected by the target model. Chat templates differ substantially across model architectures. Even checkpoints derived from the same base model often disagree on how to format tool schemas, delimit parallel calls, or signal message boundaries. A serialized dataset artifact must therefore record the tokenizer version, template configuration, tool-formatting schema, and response-boundary policy alongside the token arrays. The true model input consists of the message sequence paired with this concrete rendering configuration.

In schematic form, a multi-turn tool-calling example follows the structure shown below. The delimiter strings are illustrative placeholders, as each model family defines its own special tokens. Here, the system segment defines the task contract and tool definitions, the assistant segment emits an optional reasoning trace followed by two parallel tool calls with unique identifiers, and each tool segment returns an observation matched to its corresponding call identifier.

```text
<|system|> task contract; schemas for read_file(target_uri), run_tests(target) <|end|>
<|user|> Fix the connection-pool leak in src/pool.py <|end|>
<|assistant|> <|reasoning|> Reproduce the failure, then read the module. <|end_reasoning|>
  <|call id=c1|> {"name": "read_file", "arguments": {"target_uri": "src/pool.py"}} <|end_call|>
  <|call id=c2|> {"name": "run_tests", "arguments": {"target": "tests/test_pool.py"}} <|end_call|>
<|end_turn|>
<|tool id=c2|> FAILED test_release: pool exhausted <|end|>
<|tool id=c1|> ...file contents... <|end|>
<|assistant|> ...
```

In this sequence, `c2` completes before `c1`, and this runtime delivers observations in arrival order, so the listing places the `c2` reply first because that is the prompt the model actually received at its next turn. The call identifiers keep each observation bound to its original invocation regardless of that order. The error to avoid is re-sorting the replies into call order (`c1`, then `c2`) for tidiness, which would invent a prompt the model never saw. Serialization assembles tokens according to how the runtime presented the prompt to the model, whatever order that was. Reordering calls whose arguments or observations depend on one another alters the causal problem; any such permutation constitutes a synthetic data transformation that requires explicit validation. The `<|end_turn|>` token records where the policy surrendered control to the runtime loop, while all tokens enclosed between `<|tool|>` and `<|end|>` constitute external observations.

The training pipeline bundles this rendered dataset as `serialization_v1`. Its manifest couples the admitted execution records with the active rendering configuration, mapping every selected response span to its exact token offsets. Because tokenization, template injection, and string redaction can shift token boundaries (leading whitespace can merge into an adjacent special token, for example), the pipeline must re-verify all token offsets against the final rendered array. A rigorous pipeline decodes completed examples to inspect task prompts, tool bindings, span boundaries, and end-of-sequence markers. If an example fails boundary alignment or drops content, the pipeline drops the record entirely rather than patching it with synthetic filler.

Role delimiters establish protocol syntax, but they convey no runtime authority. If a model generates text that mimics a `<|tool|>` delimiter, that text remains model output under the tokenizer's grammar; the serialization pipeline must never promote unverified generations into genuine environment observations.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The rule that model output is a proposal carrying no authority until the runtime validates it is established in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-role.
:::

### One example per invocation {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-per-invocation}

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-per-turn-expansion
#| echo: false
# PER-TURN EXAMPLE EXPANSION (LEGO)
# Goal: Price one-example-per-invocation serialization against one transcript.
# Scope: Stipulated horizon; each turn adds a similar number of tokens.
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_multiple

class PerTurnExpansion:
    # 1. LOAD: stipulated horizon in turns.
    horizon = 30

    # 2. EXECUTE: prefixes of 1..H turns versus one H-turn transcript.
    per_turn_units = horizon * (horizon + 1) / 2
    transcript_units = horizon
    expansion = per_turn_units / transcript_units

    # 3. GUARD: closed form (H+1)/2.
    check(abs(expansion - (horizon + 1) / 2) < 1e-12, "Expansion is (H+1)/2")
    check(expansion > 1, "Separate examples repeat context")

    # 4. OUTPUT: consumed in the serialization prose.
    horizon_str = fmt_int(horizon)
    expansion_mult_str = fmt_multiple(expansion, precision=1)
```

Serving runtimes vary in how they manage conversational history. Some systems preserve full transcripts across iterations, while others prune earlier steps, compact intermediate context, or discard chain-of-thought scratchpads between turns to reduce KV cache footprints. A single concatenated transcript provides a faithful training example only when its causal attention prefixes match what the model actually perceived during online inference. The repair agent's own runtime compacts history once the working set crosses its watermark, so a turn delivered after compaction saw a digest, not the raw turns that a concatenated transcript would place before it. When serving prunes or compresses history between steps, each invocation must instead be serialized as an independent training example containing its exact delivered prefix.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Watermark-triggered compaction, which replaces earlier turns with a digest between invocations, is established in @sec-vol3-context-engineering-compaction.
:::

This independence incurs a substantial computational penalty, and its arithmetic is the triangular sum that already priced an append-only trajectory at serving time (@eq-vol3-trajectory-resend), now paid in stored training tokens. If a trajectory spans $\TurnHorizon$ turns and each turn contributes roughly $\TurnAppendLength$ tokens, the example for turn $\TurnIndex$ spans approximately $\TurnIndex\,\TurnAppendLength$ tokens. Serializing all $\TurnHorizon$ invocations independently requires $\TurnAppendLength\,\TurnHorizon(\TurnHorizon+1)/2$ tokens, compared to just $\TurnHorizon\,\TurnAppendLength$ tokens for a unified transcript, an expansion factor of $(\TurnHorizon+1)/2$. Over a stipulated horizon of `{python} PerTurnExpansion.horizon_str` turns, serializing each invocation separately multiplies the required token volume by `{python} PerTurnExpansion.expansion_mult_str`. An agent system's history-retention policy is therefore a primary engineering constraint when sizing training compute. The same fidelity rule covers the model's own reasoning text. If serving discards an earlier turn's rationale before the next invocation, the reconstructed prefix for that invocation omits it too; whether retained rationale then becomes a target or stays context is a separate choice (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-optional-rationale).

With `serialization_v1` assembled, the pipeline defines the tokenized sequences, their conditioning evidence, and the response spans selected during curation. The remaining challenge is determining which token predictions contribute to the training loss. Unmasked cross-entropy over entire multi-turn sequences would inadvertently penalize the model for failing to predict external tool outputs or user messages. Observation loss masking converts the curated span boundaries into aligned prediction targets while preserving necessary observations as conditioning context.

## Observation Loss Masking {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-loss-masking}

A data loader that naively selects every assistant token trains the model on malformed proposals alongside their subsequent corrections, unraveling careful curation decisions. Worse, a loader that computes loss across all tokens asks the policy to predict external environment responses. Serialization structures the input sequence into tokens, but the loss mask determines which of those tokens generate parameter updates.

### The masked objective {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-masked-objective}

Let $\SerializedTrainingExample=(\SequenceToken_1,\ldots,\SequenceToken_{\SequenceLength})$ be one serialized example, with an initial context or boundary token at $\SequenceToken_1$. Let $\EligibleTargetPositionSet\subseteq\{2,\ldots,\SequenceLength\}$ contain the eligible policy-token positions selected for imitation. Position eligibility depends on admitted response spans and the specific training objective rather than token authorship alone. The mask is $\PositionLossMask_{t}=\IndicatorFunction\{\TokenIndex\in\EligibleTargetPositionSet\}$, with $\PositionLossMask_1=0$. For an example with at least one selected target, the mean masked cross-entropy is

$$\MaskedFinetuningLoss(\ModelParameters)=-\frac{1}{\ActiveTargetTokenCount}\sum_{t=2}^{\SequenceLength}\PositionLossMask_{t}\log\Policy(\SequenceToken_t\mid \TokenPrefix),\qquad \ActiveTargetTokenCount=\sum_{t=2}^{\SequenceLength}\PositionLossMask_{t}>0.$$ {#eq-vol3-sft-masked-objective}

Each selected token is predicted from the preceding prefix. During training, the model conditions on the recorded sequence prefix, including earlier actions, observations, and admitted mistakes, rather than sampling fresh rollouts at each step. This training regime is **teacher forcing**\index{Teacher forcing!definition}[^fn-teacher-forcing-origin] [@williams1989learning]. It allows recovery prefixes that contain historical failures to serve as valid conditioning contexts, provided the trajectory satisfies the curation contract.

[^fn-teacher-forcing-origin]: **Teacher Forcing**: Williams and Zipser named the technique in 1989 for recurrent networks, feeding the recorded target back as the next input instead of the network's own output. Because every prefix is recorded rather than generated, a causal model computes all of an example's next-token predictions in one parallel forward pass, which is why imitating a trajectory costs one pass per example rather than one sampled rollout per decision.

In the running repair trajectory, `target_mask_v1` maps reviewed response spans directly onto the tokens emitted by `serialization_v1`, distinguishing target tokens from conditioning context (@tbl-vol3-loss-masking-strata). Modifying a tokenizer vocabulary, adjusting chat formatting templates, or transforming text inputs inevitably alters token alignments. Consequently, the pipeline must regenerate and validate masks against the exact serialization output rather than copying offsets across pipeline stages.

| Token segment                                              | Target policy for this imitation objective                                                 | What remains as conditioning input                                                   |
|:-----------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Prompt and supplied tool contracts                         | $\PositionLossMask_{t}=0$                                                                  | The actual task, current interfaces, and supplied constraints                        |
| Selected policy response                                   | $\PositionLossMask_{t}=1$ on its admitted target positions                                 | Earlier tokens of the response and its available prefix                              |
| Unselected policy response, including the refused proposal | $\PositionLossMask_{t}=0$                                                                  | History needed to interpret a selected correction                                    |
| Tool or environment observation                            | $\PositionLossMask_{t}=0$                                                                  | Delivered results, errors, and evidence available before the next response           |
| Optional authorized rationale                              | Chosen by the declared target policy                                                       | Retained rationale remains visible whether or not it is selected                     |
| Termination boundary                                       | Select an authentic policy-generated terminator when teaching the selected response to end | Do not substitute a tool-role boundary or invent a terminator for a cut-off response |

: **Loss Masking by Token Segment**: The loss mask specifies which serialized tokens generate gradient updates. It acts as an optimization filter rather than an attention barrier or provenance record. {#tbl-vol3-loss-masking-strata}

When an example contains no selected targets ($\ActiveTargetTokenCount=0$), the loss in @eq-vol3-sft-masked-objective is undefined. The data loader must either drop such examples from the supervised objective or process them under an explicit fallback policy; it must never record them as completed demonstrations. Batch-level weighting strategies across heterogeneous examples present distinct numerical trade-offs, developed in @sec-vol3-fine-tuning-batching.

::: {#dfn-action-loss-masking .callout-definition title="Observation loss masking"}

***Observation loss masking***\index{Observation loss masking!definition}\index{Supervised fine-tuning!loss masking} excludes supplied observations from the direct token-prediction loss while retaining the permitted observation context needed to train selected policy responses.

1. **Significance**: Focuses the optimization objective strictly on the policy's conditional distribution $\Policy(\TrajectoryAction_{t}\mid \TrajectoryState_{t})$. Consequently, verbose environment output cannot dilute the gradient signal for policy actions, regardless of how much sequence context observations consume (notebook \ref{nbk-15-gradient-budget-and-compute-allocation} quantifies this dilution).
2. **Distinction**: Masked tokens remain in the input context and participate in self-attention; only their next-token loss terms are omitted. Furthermore, policy authorship alone does not qualify a token as a target: rejected attempts or toxic actions require masking even when generated by an assistant role.
3. **Common pitfall**: Selecting an entire multi-turn tool exchange simply because the tool call succeeded, inadvertently training the model to predict external environment responses.

:::

### Causal label alignment {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-label-alignment}

In causal autoregressive models,[^fn-causal-mask-shift] the hidden state at input index $\TokenIndex-1$ generates the logits that predict token $\SequenceToken_t$. The data loader must therefore align the prediction logits at $\TokenIndex-1$ with target label $\SequenceToken_t$ and target mask $\PositionLossMask_{t}$, rather than attaching the mask of input token $\SequenceToken_{t-1}$. @Tbl-vol3-mask-causal-shift illustrates this boundary alignment. Because several distributed training frameworks perform this causal shift internally within their loss functions, applying a manual shift inside the data loader can silently misalign targets by one token across the entire corpus. Inspect the aligned labels and predicted tokens on a synthetic short example before launching large-scale training runs.

[^fn-causal-mask-shift]: **Causal Self-Attention**: Causal masking in Transformer decoders restricts each token from attending to subsequent positions [@vaswani2017]. This triangular attention structure allows a single forward pass over an input sequence of length $\SequenceLength$ to compute all next-token predictions in parallel. It also enforces the label shift: the network predicts $\SequenceToken_t$ using only the representation formed at $\TokenIndex-1$.

| Logits computed from a prefix ending at…          | Next-token label                          | Target mask |
|:--------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:------------|
| The final supplied prompt token                   | First token of a selected policy response | $1$         |
| The final content token of that selected response | Its authentic policy-generated end token  | $1$         |
| The end token before a delivered tool observation | First token of that observation           | $0$         |

: **The Causal Label Shift at a Tool Boundary**: Target selection applies to the predicted token rather than the input token driving the hidden state. Exact boundary encodings depend on the serialized chat template. {#tbl-vol3-mask-causal-shift}

Let $\VocabularyTokenLogit_{t-1,\VocabularyToken}$ denote the logit for vocabulary token $\VocabularyToken$ produced from $\TokenPrefix$, using an ordinary softmax and no label smoothing. Differentiating @eq-vol3-sft-masked-objective gives

$$\frac{\partial\MaskedFinetuningLoss}{\partial \VocabularyTokenLogit_{t-1,\VocabularyToken}}=\frac{\PositionLossMask_{t}}{\ActiveTargetTokenCount}\left(\Policy(\VocabularyToken\mid \TokenPrefix)-\IndicatorFunction\{\VocabularyToken=\SequenceToken_t\}\right).$$

When $\PositionLossMask_{t}=0$, the next-token prediction at position $\TokenIndex-1$ yields zero direct loss derivative. The token nevertheless shapes subsequent representations through causal attention layers, allowing gradients backpropagated from downstream active losses to adjust the parameters that encode it. The model conditions on tool outputs without expending capacity attempting to synthesize them. This mechanism underpins verified trajectory post-training (principle \ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training}) at token-level precision.

A deployed agent trajectory records an interleaved dialogue between two distinct systems: the agent policy and the external environment. Training without observation masking forces a single parameter set to approximate two conflicting distributions simultaneously:

1. The **agent policy** $\Policy(\TrajectoryAction_{t}\mid \TrajectoryState_{t})$, mapping historical observations and instructions to deliberate tool calls or answers.
2. An **environment dynamics model** $\EnvironmentTransitionDistribution(\TrajectoryState_{t+1}\mid \TrajectoryState_{t}, \TrajectoryAction_{t})$, predicting outputs returned by arbitrary shells, database engines, or remote APIs.

Because real tools execute directly during deployment and supply ground-truth outputs, tasking the policy with predicting environment returns wastes model capacity.

Supervising the environment distribution introduces two severe systems failures:

1. **Loss dilution**\index{Loss dilution!definition}: Under standard token-averaged cross-entropy, unmasking inflates the normalization denominator from $\ActiveTargetTokenCount$ to the number of causal prediction terms, $\SequenceLength-1$, because the initial stored boundary has no preceding-position prediction. As a result, the effective gradient scale on critical decision tokens collapses proportionally to the selected fraction of predicted positions (computed in notebook \ref{nbk-15-gradient-budget-and-compute-allocation}). The loss budget then goes to runtime artifacts (file paths, stack traces, compiler dumps, and raw JSON payloads), which pull on the average in two directions. Repetitive parts such as echoed schemas, boilerplate headers, and repeated paths are easy to predict and drag the averaged loss down; novel parts such as a fresh stack trace or unseen file contents are hard to predict and swamp the gradient. Either way, the averaged number stops measuring the policy.
2. **Role confusion**\index{Role confusion!definition}: When trained to predict tokens following a tool invocation, the policy learns that tool outputs naturally succeed tool calls within the same autoregressive stream. In production, such a model can continue past its own tool call and write a fabricated tool result instead of ending the turn with the stop reason that hands control back to the runtime. Because the runtime separates generated text from authenticated environment observations (@sec-vol3-fine-tuning-serialization), it discards the fabricated result, so every such turn burns output budget on tokens that are thrown away and can stall the trajectory until the runtime intervenes.

The full repair record selects three responses (`e3`, `e4`, and `e6`). In the simplified view of @fig-vol3-loss-masking, which leaves out the schema request `e3` and its returned schema, only two of the seven segments shown, the corrected tool call and the final response, carry an active mask ($\PositionLossMask_{t}=1$) and receive direct imitation loss. The prompt, task statement, refused proposal, rejection message, and tool result carry $\PositionLossMask_{t}=0$ and remain conditioning context. Gradients from later selected targets still update the parameters that encode them.

::: {#fig-vol3-loss-masking fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Observation Loss Masking**: The mask over a simplified view of the serialized repair example that omits the schema request (selected) and its returned schema (context). Of the segments shown, only the corrected tool call and the final response carry $\PositionLossMask_{t}=1$ and receive a direct loss term. The prompt, task, refused proposal, rejection message, and tool result carry $\PositionLossMask_{t}=0$, yet every one of them is still read through attention, so gradients from later selected targets update the parameters that encode it. Selecting only policy responses fits the policy's conditional distribution; unmasking the observations would also ask the same weights to fit the environment's." fig-alt="Seven serialized segments placed left to right in order, each in one of three lanes by author. The supplied lane holds prompt and contracts and task statement. The policy lane, labeled pi theta of a t given s t, holds a dashed refused proposal, the corrected tool call, and the final response. The environment lane, labeled p of s t plus 1 given s t and a t, holds the rejection message and the tool result. A loss mask row beneath reads zero for every segment except the corrected tool call and the final response, which are filled and read one. A green attention line runs from those two mask cells back to the first segment, touching every earlier segment, labeled gradients from selected targets reach every earlier segment."}
![](images/svg/fig-vol3-loss-masking.svg)
:::

Observation masking eliminates both pathologies at the loss level. A validation loss curve cannot reveal how often an unmasked model fabricates environment outputs in practice; that failure mode emerges only during interactive, closed-loop evaluation. While predicting environment transitions is a legitimate goal when training world models or offline tool simulators, it conflicts with the policy imitation objective required for autonomous agents.

### Selected targets and compute {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-selected-targets}

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/vol3_sft_margin_targets.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="One horizontal stacked bar. A long green segment labeled observations 77.1% fills most of it, a gray segment labeled ctx follows, and a thin dark segment at the right end is labeled targets 4.9%."}

*Observations fill 77.1 percent of the input; the loss sits on 4.9 percent.*
:::

The count of selected positions $\ActiveTargetTokenCount$ establishes the denominator of the loss function and dictates the gradient magnitude assigned to each target token. In agent workflows, extensive tool outputs frequently consume the vast majority of sequence memory while serving as conditioning context for a concise corrective action. Comparing selected targets against the number of causal prediction terms reveals the exact dilution factor an unmasked objective would impose; their share of stored input instead measures occupancy. Notebook \ref{nbk-15-gradient-budget-and-compute-allocation} quantifies these allocations across two alternative target policies evaluated on the same trajectory.

```{python}
#| label: lego-15-selected-target-accounting
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SELECTED TARGET ACCOUNTING (LEGO)
# │ Context: @nbk-15-gradient-budget-and-compute-allocation.
# │ Goal: Separate stored positions from eligible imitation targets.
# │ Show: Two masks on one hypothetical input retain identical context.
# │ How: Sum segment counts; exclude unselected responses; count targets.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent

class SelectedTargetAccounting:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Hypothetical Token Counts) ────────────────────────────
    prompt = 1_200  # includes the initial context/boundary position
    task = 184
    optional_rationale = 1_400  # available, authorized, reviewed text
    response = 960  # response content and authentic terminators
    observation = 12_640
    unselected_response = 160  # retained as context, not desired targets
    checkpoint_observation = 30_000  # given for the reader's estimate in the checkpoint

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (One Input, Two Target Policies) ────────────────────
    stored = prompt + task + optional_rationale + response + observation
    selected_response = response - unselected_response
    with_rationale = selected_response + optional_rationale
    without_rationale = selected_response
    observation_share = observation / stored
    with_share = with_rationale / stored
    without_share = without_rationale / stored
    context_only_with = stored - with_rationale
    context_only_without = stored - without_rationale
    # The first stored boundary has no preceding-position prediction.
    predicted = stored - 1
    dilution_without = predicted / without_rationale
    dilution_with = predicted / with_rationale
    stored_double_obs = stored + observation
    predicted_double_obs = stored_double_obs - 1
    dilution_double_obs = predicted_double_obs / without_rationale
    unselected_vs_selected = unselected_response / selected_response

    # ┌── 3. ASSERT (Partitions and Positive Denominators) ───────────────
    check(0 <= unselected_response < response, "valid response selection")
    check(stored == 16_384, "declared input partition")
    check(0 < without_rationale <= with_rationale <= predicted, "valid prediction targets")
    check(predicted == stored - 1 > 0, "initial boundary is not predicted")
    check(predicted_double_obs == stored_double_obs - 1 > predicted, "expanded prediction count")
    check(with_rationale + context_only_with == stored, "first partition")
    check(without_rationale + context_only_without == stored, "second partition")
    check(with_rationale - without_rationale == optional_rationale, "mask difference")
    check(dilution_without > dilution_with > 1, "masking concentrates weight")
    check(dilution_double_obs > dilution_without, "longer observations dilute more")
    check(checkpoint_observation > observation, "checkpoint grows the observations")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Computed Display Exports) ───────────────────────────
    prompt_str = fmt_int(prompt)
    task_str = fmt_int(task)
    rationale_str = fmt_int(optional_rationale)
    response_str = fmt_int(response)
    observation_str = fmt_int(observation)
    unselected_str = fmt_int(unselected_response)
    stored_str = fmt_int(stored)
    predicted_str = fmt_int(predicted)
    observation_share_str = fmt_percent(observation_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    with_str = fmt_int(with_rationale)
    without_str = fmt_int(without_rationale)
    with_share_str = fmt_percent(with_share, precision=1, style="symbol")
    without_share_str = fmt_percent(without_share, precision=1, style="symbol")
    selected_response_str = fmt_int(selected_response)
    dilution_without_mult_str = fmt_multiple(dilution_without, precision=1)
    dilution_with_mult_str = fmt_multiple(dilution_with, precision=1)
    dilution_double_obs_mult_str = fmt_multiple(dilution_double_obs, precision=1)
    unselected_vs_selected_str = fmt_percent(unselected_vs_selected, precision=0, style="prose")
    checkpoint_observation_str = fmt_int(checkpoint_observation)
```

::: {#nbk-15-gradient-budget-and-compute-allocation .callout-notebook title="Stored tokens and selected targets"}

**Problem**: A hypothetical serialized example has the segment counts in @tbl-vol3-mask-token-inventory. Its curation record excludes some policy-response positions from imitation while retaining them as context. If the optional rationale is either selected or kept as context only, how many positions receive direct loss, what fraction of the stored input do they occupy, and by how much would an unmasked loss dilute each of them?

| Input segment                                             |                                       Stored tokens |
|:----------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------:|
| System prompt and schemas, including the initial boundary |      `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.prompt_str` |
| Task statement                                            |        `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.task_str` |
| Optional authorized rationale                             |   `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.rationale_str` |
| Other policy responses, including authentic end tokens    |    `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.response_str` |
| Delivered observations                                    | `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.observation_str` |

: **Hypothetical Input Inventory**: These disjoint counts include every stored position. They are not measurements of the shared repair run. {#tbl-vol3-mask-token-inventory}

**Variables**: Exactly `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.unselected_str` of the other-policy-response positions belong to the refused proposal and stay context; every other response position is selected. The rationale is reviewed for either target policy, both policies see the same input, the initial position belongs to the prompt, and there is no padding.

**Math**: The disjoint segments sum to `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.stored_str` stored tokens, of which observations occupy `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.observation_share_str`. Removing the refused positions leaves `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.response_str` $-$ `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.unselected_str` $=$ `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.selected_response_str` selected response targets, and selecting the rationale adds `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.rationale_str` more. The first stored boundary has no preceding-position prediction, so an unmasked causal average divides by `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.predicted_str` prediction terms instead of $\ActiveTargetTokenCount$. Each selected target's coefficient therefore shrinks by `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.predicted_str`/`{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.selected_response_str`, a factor of `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.dilution_without_mult_str` (`{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.dilution_with_mult_str` when the rationale is selected). Under each target policy, @tbl-vol3-mask-target-counts sets $\ActiveTargetTokenCount$ against the stored input it is drawn from.

| Target policy                                          |   Selected positions, $\ActiveTargetTokenCount$ |                        Selected share of stored input |
|:-------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------:|------------------------------------------------------:|
| Selected responses plus reviewed rationale             |    `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.with_str` |    `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.with_share_str` |
| Selected responses; rationale retained as context only | `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.without_str` | `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.without_share_str` |

: **Two Target Policies on One Input**: Excluding a segment from the objective does not shorten the conditioning sequence. {#tbl-vol3-mask-target-counts}

**Result**: Both masks place the whole loss on a small minority of stored positions and leave the context identical; they differ only in whether the rationale is a target.

**Systems insight**: Because the dilution factor scales inversely with the selected fraction of predicted positions, it expands rapidly as environment interactions accumulate. Doubling the observation volume while holding response lengths constant escalates dilution from `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.dilution_without_mult_str` to `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.dilution_double_obs_mult_str`. Consequently, observation masking becomes increasingly essential as agents tackle deep, tool-intensive reasoning traces. Notice, however, that masking yields negligible reductions in FLOPs: every masked token must still pass through causal attention layers to form context for subsequent predictions. Only the final language model head projection and cross-entropy loss computation can be bypassed at masked positions.

:::

Recorded repair trajectories show that the hypothetical inventory's proportions are realistic. @Fig-vol3-trajectory-composition splits the transcripts of five published agent configurations on the same repository-repair tasks [@jimenez2024swebench] by the role that produced each message.

```{python}
#| label: calc-vol3-trajectory-composition
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MEASURED TRAJECTORY COMPOSITION (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-vol3-trajectory-composition and the paragraph after it.
# │ Goal: Ground the hypothetical mask inventory in recorded trajectories.
# │ Show: Range of observation and model-output shares across configurations.
# │ How:  Literature.SweBenchTrajectories; characters pooled per
# │       configuration, each message counted once.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Literature
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_int, fmt_percent

class TrajectoryComposition:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    runs = Literature.SweBenchTrajectories.entries

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    totals = {}
    for _r in runs:
        _t = totals.setdefault((_r["scaffold"], _r["model"]), [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0])
        _t[0] += _r["model_chars"]
        _t[1] += _r["obs_chars"]
        _t[2] += _r["prompt_chars"]
        _t[3] += _r["total_chars"]
    obs_shares = sorted(v[1] / v[3] for v in totals.values())
    model_shares = sorted(v[0] / v[3] for v in totals.values())

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    check(obs_shares[0] > 0.5, "Prose says observations are the majority in every configuration")
    check(model_shares[-1] < 1 / 3, "Prose says model output is under a third everywhere")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_configs_str = fmt_int(len(totals))
    n_runs_str = fmt_int(len(runs))
    obs_lo_str = fmt_int(round(100 * obs_shares[0]))
    obs_hi_str = fmt_percent(round(obs_shares[-1], 2), precision=0, style="prose")
    model_lo_str = fmt_int(round(100 * model_shares[0]))
    model_hi_str = fmt_percent(round(model_shares[-1], 2), precision=0, style="prose")
```

:::: {#fig-vol3-trajectory-composition fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Observations Dominate Recorded Trajectories**: Share of transcript characters by the role that produced them, pooled over every run of each configuration and counting each message once. Prompt covers the system message, demonstrations, and task statement; observations are tool and environment output; model output is everything the model generated, the only region from which training targets can be selected. Characters stand in for tokens because the configurations use different tokenizers. Trajectories from @jimenez2024swebench submissions." fig-alt="Five horizontal stacked bars, one per agent configuration, each spanning 0 to 100 percent of transcript characters. Each bar has a gray prompt segment, a long green observation segment between about 56 and 72 percent, and a dark model-output segment between about 12 and 31 percent, with the percentage printed inside each wide segment."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MEASURED TRAJECTORY COMPOSITION (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-vol3-trajectory-composition
# │
# │ Goal: Show how much of a recorded trajectory is observation.
# │ Show: Stacked prompt / observation / model-output shares per configuration.
# │ How: Literature.SweBenchTrajectories (MLSysIM); book_style.setup_plot().
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Literature
from binder.tools.figures import style as book_style

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = book_style.setup_plot(figsize=(8, 3.2))
totals = {}
for r in Literature.SweBenchTrajectories.entries:
    t = totals.setdefault((r["scaffold"], r["model"]), [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0])
    t[0] += r["prompt_chars"]
    t[1] += r["obs_chars"]
    t[2] += r["model_chars"]
    t[3] += r["total_chars"]
labels = [f"{s}, {m}" for s, m in totals]
segments = [
    ("Prompt", COLORS["grid"], COLORS["primary"]),
    ("Observations", COLORS["GreenLine"], "white"),
    ("Model output", COLORS["primary"], "white"),
]
left = [0.0] * len(totals)
for j, (name, color, text_color) in enumerate(segments):
    share = [100 * v[j] / v[3] for v in totals.values()]
    ax.barh(labels, share, left=left, color=color, label=name, edgecolor="white", lw=0.8)
    for i, (x0, w) in enumerate(zip(left, share)):
        if w >= 9:
            ax.text(x0 + w / 2, i, f"{w:.0f}%", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8, color=text_color)
    left = [a + b for a, b in zip(left, share)]
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
ax.set_xlabel("Share of transcript characters (%)")
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_axisbelow(True)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8.5, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.24), ncol=3)
plt.show()
plt.close()
```

::::

Across the `{python} TrajectoryComposition.n_configs_str` configurations and `{python} TrajectoryComposition.n_runs_str` runs, observations make up `{python} TrajectoryComposition.obs_lo_str` to `{python} TrajectoryComposition.obs_hi_str` of the transcript, and model output only `{python} TrajectoryComposition.model_lo_str` to `{python} TrajectoryComposition.model_hi_str`. These shares count each message once. Serializing one example per invocation repeats the growing prefix in every example, so the observation share of the stored training input is larger still, approaching the inventory's proportion. The mask is therefore not a refinement applied to a few verbose tool calls; in recorded repair work it decides the fate of most of the sequence.

### Optional rationale as target or context {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-optional-rationale}

Many agent datasets incorporate intermediate reasoning traces, such as chain-of-thought scratchpads or tool-use plans. Deciding how to supervise this intermediate text requires choosing between three distinct data-loading regimes (@tbl-vol3-reasoning-mask-regimes). Supervising the rationale trains the model to generate its own reasoning before invoking tools. Retaining the rationale under a loss mask treats the reasoning as supplied conditioning context, training the model to act upon plans provided by an external orchestrator or user. Stripping the rationale entirely fundamentally alters the conditional distribution by forcing the policy to act directly from context alone.

Formally, given context prefix $\TurnContext_{t}$, rationale tokens $\RationaleTokens$, and action tokens $\ResponseActionTokens=(\ResponseActionTokens_1,\ldots,\ResponseActionTokens_n)$, response-only supervision models the conditional distribution $\Policy(\ResponseActionTokens_j\mid \TurnContext_{t}, \RationaleTokens, \ActionTokenPrefix)$. If the production serving environment does not provide $\RationaleTokens$, the deployed model must evaluate $\Policy(\ResponseActionTokens_j\mid \TurnContext_{t}, \ActionTokenPrefix)$. Because these represent mathematically distinct conditional distributions, omitting rationale at training time represents an explicit distillation experiment that must be validated directly against the unconditioned serving target.

| Treatment                                        | Input and direct targets                                                                                                                           | Serving question to evaluate                                                                          |
|:-------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Select reviewed rationale                        | Retain $[\TurnContext_{t},\RationaleTokens,\ResponseActionTokens]$; selected $\RationaleTokens$ and $\ResponseActionTokens$ positions receive loss | Does generated rationale improve the declared outcomes enough to justify its output and latency cost? |
| Retain rationale as context only                 | Retain $[\TurnContext_{t},\RationaleTokens,\ResponseActionTokens]$; only selected $\ResponseActionTokens$ positions receive loss                   | How will appropriate rationale become available, and how do errors in it affect the response?         |
| Remove rationale under a reviewed transformation | Use $[\TurnContext_{t},\ResponseActionTokens]$; selected $\ResponseActionTokens$ positions receive loss                                            | Does the policy perform adequately without the removed conditioning information?                      |

: **Rationale Treatment Changes Targets or Inputs**: The choice requires a compatible serving protocol and evaluation, not a universal model-size threshold. {#tbl-vol3-reasoning-mask-regimes}

At inference time, an external planning agent or the policy's own autoregressive generator can supply the required reasoning text. When the model generates its own rationale, runtime text inevitably diverges from the training demonstration; downstream evaluation must measure this divergence. A rationale segment merits target status only when the system architecture explicitly requires the deployed policy to synthesize its own thoughts under operational latency and token budgets.

### Termination and truncated responses {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-termination}

To teach an agent when to yield control, the training loss must include the authentic policy-generated termination token (such as `<|eom_id|>` or `<|im_end|>`) at the end of each selected response. Host frameworks often insert their own control delimiters to demarcate incoming tool payloads; data loaders must never confuse these host delimiters with genuine policy stop tokens. Excluding termination tokens from the loss mask deprives the model of direct supervision on when to stop. Without that supervision, the policy can generate past the end of its action until the output limit cuts it off. Such calls return `TRUNCATED` rather than `COMPLETED`, so the runtime's quarantining rule withholds a proposal that may have been correct.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The normalized `TRUNCATED` status and the quarantining rule that withholds an incomplete candidate are established in @sec-vol3-foundation-model-status-envelope.
:::

Truncated responses, where an output was cut short by a context window or a timeout, present a dangerous edge case. A common pipeline flaw is appending a synthetic end-of-turn token to an incomplete response, which trains the policy to end a turn on a partial command. That is the training-side twin of the hazard the quarantining rule blocks at serving time, where a truncated `rm -rf` argument still parses as a complete and broader command. The training-side version is worse, because a policy that has learned to emit the terminator after a partial command produces a `COMPLETED` status, which the quarantining rule admits. When encountering truncated turns, engineering pipelines should adopt one of two sound strategies:

1. **Conservative exclusion**: Mask the truncated turn entirely ($\PositionLossMask_{t}=0$) while preserving preceding successful turns in the trajectory.
2. **Prefix-only supervision**: Supervise the valid initial tokens of the truncated turn up to the truncation point, but strictly omit any terminating token.

Whenever trajectories undergo truncation, sliding-window packing, or template transformations, the data pipeline must recompute target masks and verify that $\ActiveTargetTokenCount > 0$. Robust training loaders implement automated unit assertions on critical boundaries: the first token of an agent response, the closing turn terminator, the transition into tool observations, rejected recovery attempts, and truncated sequences. Validating these boundaries guarantees that the training engine optimizes the exact supervised objective declared by the curation policy.

::: {#chk-15-loss-masking .callout-checkpoint title="Defend the target mask"}

- [ ] **Curation to tokens**: Which of `e2`, `e3`, the tool reply to `e3`, `e4`, and `e6` carry $\PositionLossMask_{t}=1$ under `recovery_targets_v1`, and what would training the others teach?
- [ ] **Causal alignment**: Which input position's logits predict the first selected response token, and which token's mask must accompany that prediction?
- [ ] **Masked vs. removed**: How can a masked observation affect parameter updates through a later selected response?
- [ ] **Dilution estimate**: If the observations in notebook \ref{nbk-15-gradient-budget-and-compute-allocation} grew to `{python} SelectedTargetAccounting.checkpoint_observation_str` tokens with every other segment unchanged, by roughly what factor would an unmasked token average dilute each selected response target, and why would masking save far less compute than that factor?
- [ ] **Termination**: A response was cut off at the output limit. Which of its positions remain eligible for selection, and what must the loader refuse to append?

:::

With per-example loss masking in place, the training loader enforces the exact boundary between conditioning context and imitation targets. Production training, however, batches heterogeneous trajectories across varying sequence lengths and device topologies. The batching and collation mechanisms must uphold this target contract without silently skewing loss weights across sequence lengths.

## Batching Variable-Length Trajectories {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-batching}

Consider a batch where a lengthy debugging and code repair trace shares a single training buffer with a brief, unrelated file lookup. Under an ordinary lower-triangular causal mask, the lookup can attend directly to the repair trace's intermediate file contents and tool outputs, context that the lookup policy will never encounter during online inference. Under token averaging, the multi-turn repair trace will also outweigh the brief lookup by the exact ratio of their active target tokens.

Constructing a batch of variable-length trajectories therefore forces two coupled systems decisions: how much gradient weight each trajectory exerts on the optimization objective, and how multiple sequences share physical buffer memory without leaking information across sequence boundaries. Sequence packing is strictly a memory layout optimization; a correct implementation preserves both the mathematically specified loss and the causal isolation of each sequence's predictive context.

### Loss normalization across variable-length examples {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-loss-normalization}

Let a batch contain $\BatchSize$ examples. Example $\BatchExampleIndex$ has stored length $\SequenceLength^{(\BatchExampleIndex)}$, including context, and ${\ActiveTargetTokenCount}_{\BatchExampleIndex}>0$ selected target tokens under the preceding section's mask. Let $\LossFunction_{\BatchExampleIndex}$ be its mean masked negative log-likelihood. Two batch objectives are

$$\TokenAveragedBatchLoss=
\sum_{\BatchExampleIndex=1}^{\BatchSize}\frac{{\ActiveTargetTokenCount}_{\BatchExampleIndex}}{\sum_{k=1}^{\BatchSize}{\ActiveTargetTokenCount}_k}\LossFunction_{\BatchExampleIndex},$$ {#eq-vol3-loss-token}

$$\ExampleAveragedBatchLoss=\frac{1}{\BatchSize}\sum_{\BatchExampleIndex=1}^{\BatchSize}\LossFunction_{\BatchExampleIndex}.$$ {#eq-vol3-loss-example}

**Token averaging**\index{Token averaging!definition} in @eq-vol3-loss-token assigns equal coefficients to selected token losses. **Example averaging**\index{Example averaging!definition} in @eq-vol3-loss-example assigns equal coefficients to example means. Both count selected targets, never context or padding. A record with no selected targets supplies no $\LossFunction_{\BatchExampleIndex}$ and is excluded from either objective.

These normalization coefficients govern the loss function directly, though realized gradient magnitudes also depend on prediction errors and parameter sensitivities. Example averaging equalizes serialized example means, not completed interactions or underlying tasks; one example may represent a single invocation. In contrast, token averaging weights each example proportionally to its active target count.

This distinction becomes critical when trajectory serialization splits a multi-turn interaction into separate training records. If one of $\BatchSize$ initial examples becomes $\TurnHorizon$ per-invocation examples while every other example remains once, example averaging changes that trajectory's aggregate share from $1/\BatchSize$ to $\TurnHorizon/(\BatchSize-1+\TurnHorizon)$. It has $\TurnHorizon$ times each unsplit example's share, rather than $\TurnHorizon$ times its former normalized share. Under token averaging, the trajectory's aggregate share remains unchanged only if its selected targets form a disjoint partition, each turn is selected once, and the other batch members and their targets stay unchanged. Repeating prefix context alone does not repeat active targets. Data sampling, trajectory segmentation, and loss normalization therefore jointly dictate how underlying agent capabilities are weighted during optimization. A corpus mixture specified in selected target tokens, the unit in which @sec-vol3-trajectory-curation-token-accounting fixes class shares, reaches the update unchanged only under token averaging; example averaging, or a per-invocation split that does not partition the selected targets disjointly, changes the realized mixture. Writing out the coefficients each objective places on an example mean and on a single selected token (@tbl-vol3-loss-normalization-comparison) makes the difference exact.

| Property                                                         | Token averaging                                                                     | Example averaging                                               |
|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|
| Coefficient on example mean $\LossFunction_{\BatchExampleIndex}$ | ${\ActiveTargetTokenCount}_{\BatchExampleIndex}/\sum_k {\ActiveTargetTokenCount}_k$ | $1/\BatchSize$                                                  |
| Coefficient on a selected token loss                             | $1/\sum_k {\ActiveTargetTokenCount}_k$                                              | $1/(\BatchSize {\ActiveTargetTokenCount}_{\BatchExampleIndex})$ |
| Quantity treated equally                                         | Selected token losses                                                               | Example mean losses                                             |

: **Loss normalization for variable-length examples**: Equal coefficients specify the objective, not equal gradient norms or equal representation of underlying tasks. {#tbl-vol3-loss-normalization-comparison}

The mathematical equivalence in @tbl-vol3-loss-normalization-comparison requires careful distributed accounting. A large batch is rarely processed in one piece. It is split into microbatches (slices processed one after another before a single parameter update) and spread across data-parallel workers (each holding a copy of the model and processing its own share of the batch). Computing a true global token average requires summing active token losses and token counts across all microbatches and workers before dividing. Averaging local microbatch means directly produces an accurate token average only when active token counts match across all microbatches; otherwise, the workers must combine their raw sums and counts before taking the ratio.

### Example isolation in packed buffers {#sec-vol3-fine-tuning-packed-isolation}

::: {#dfn-sequence-packing .callout-definition title="Sequence packing"}

***Sequence packing***\index{Sequence packing!definition} places several variable-length training examples in shared buffers while preserving their intended information boundaries and loss targets.

1. **Significance**: Uniform padding allocates the longest example's length to every row, reducing batch occupancy to the ratio of mean to maximum sequence length. Sequence packing reclaims this wasted capacity (notebook \ref{nbk-vol3-packing-occupancy}).
2. **Distinction**: Independent trajectories share physical memory buffers without sharing predictive context; multi-turn interactions within an individual trajectory retain access to their complete history.
3. **Common pitfall**: Applying a standard causal mask across concatenated sequences, allowing later examples to attend illegitimately to earlier ones.

:::

The file lookup from the section's opening must never read the repair trace's file contents or tool observations. Reading them would be *cross-contamination*,[^fn-packing-cross-contamination] the leak a packed layout must prevent [@krell2021efficient]. Let $\QueryBufferPosition$ and $\KeyBufferPosition$ denote buffer positions, $\QueryVector_i$ and $\KeyVector_j$ their query and key vectors, and $\AttentionHeadDimension$ the attention-head dimension. The pre-softmax attention scores $\text{score}_{i,j}$ enforce both causality and example membership:

$$\text{score}_{i,j}=\begin{cases}
\QueryVector_i\KeyVector_j^T/\sqrt{\AttentionHeadDimension} & \text{if }\operatorname{example}(\QueryBufferPosition)=\operatorname{example}(\KeyBufferPosition)\text{ and }\KeyBufferPosition\le \QueryBufferPosition,\\
-\infty & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}$$ {#eq-vol3-block-diagonal-attention}

Under an ordinary causal mask, every query in a later example can score keys in an earlier one; the block-diagonal mask sets each of those cross-example entries to $-\infty$ before the softmax, and excludes trailing padding keys the same way (@fig-vol3-block-diagonal-mask). Variable-length attention kernels [@dao2023flashattention2] enforce this without materializing a dense $-\infty$ matrix. The loader hands the kernel the example boundaries as cumulative offsets, $0$, $\PackedExampleLength_1$, $\PackedExampleLength_1+\PackedExampleLength_2$, and so on through the buffer's total length ($\BatchSize+1$ entries for $\BatchSize$ examples), so that example $\PackedExampleIndex$ occupies one contiguous interval of positions, and the kernel computes scores only for query and key pairs that fall inside the same interval. Whether a given kernel also skips the computation for cross-example blocks of the score matrix, and how much time that saves, is an implementation property to measure on the target accelerator. The mask is the correctness requirement; skipped work is a throughput bonus that must be shown, not assumed.

[^fn-packing-cross-contamination]: **Cross-Contamination**: Krell and colleagues used the term for attention and label leakage between sequences packed into one buffer, and showed that masks, position resets, and per-sequence loss handling make a packed model mathematically equivalent to the unpacked one. The equivalence is the property to test: a packed loader that trains faster but lets examples read one another has changed the learning problem, and no loss curve will show it.

::: {#fig-vol3-block-diagonal-mask fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Block-Diagonal Attention for Packed Examples**: Two independent examples share one buffer. Under an ordinary causal mask (a), every query in the second example scores keys in the first, so the second example can use context it will not have when served. The block-diagonal mask (b) keeps causal scores only inside each example and sets every cross-example entry to $-\infty$ before the softmax, as in @eq-vol3-block-diagonal-attention. The boundary offsets define the blocks; whether a kernel also skips the masked blocks is an implementation property." fig-alt="Two eight-by-eight attention grids, queries down the side and keys across the top, each split into example 1 with five positions and example 2 with three. In panel a, the lower triangle within each example is shaded as a score, the remaining upper cells are gray minus infinity, and the block where example 2 queries meet example 1 keys is shaded red and labeled leak.
